assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on the magic-wavelength idea, turned laser spectroscopy of narrow atomic transitions into the most accurate measurements ever made, at fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The work is original, conceptually clean and underpins redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and fundamental-constant tests. It fits the long Nobel line from precision spectroscopy to frequency combs.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice trapping scheme and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock; Ye drove it to the performance frontier and integrated it with combs and many-body physics. The credit is compact (two names) and fair. Optical-clock work more broadly involves many groups, but these two are the clear leaders on this credited list. Declared connection: Ye is associated with the Hall laboratory, where I spent a research stay, and I treat this only as background.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs have confirmed the clocks and compared them across continents, the interpretation is stable, and the field has matured to the point of redefinition roadmaps. Recognition is timely, arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to credit lattice clocks separately from earlier ion-clock and comb prizes
How to weigh Katori's proposal against Ye's later developments, which I only recall from general knowledge and have not verified here

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions defined a physical architecture for quantum computation, and Blatt's group turned it into working multi-qubit gates, entanglement and algorithms. Impact on quantum information science is large and lasting, and trapped-ion systems remain a leading platform.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive theoretical proposal; Blatt is the leading experimental demonstrator in Innsbruck. Other experimental groups also contributed, and ion trapping and cooling were already recognised in 2012, so the allocation is plausible but not free of overlap.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent groups over three decades, with commercial systems as further evidence. The timing is mature, although the 2012 prize narrows the remaining novelty.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for manipulating single quantum systems
Whether the experimental credit should include other leaders not on this list

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the superfluid-Mott transition and quantum-gas microscopy, created tunable analogue quantum simulators of Hubbard-type models. This is highly original atomic physics with clear lasting impact on many-body physics. As an atomic physicist I regard it as one of the field's major achievements.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and collaborators) proposed the Hubbard-model realisation; Bloch and Greiner carried out the decisive experiments, including the Mott transition and single-site-resolved imaging. Cirac is also credited on the list, but the three chosen names give the cleanest theory-plus-experiment split. The Mott transition credit may also involve Hänsch and Greiner's earlier collaborations, which I do not resolve here.
assessment.maturity: Many groups have reproduced and extended the results. The field is mature, and quantum simulation is now broad. Overlap with the BEC prize of 2001 and with other quantum-gas candidates requires care.
uncertainties: Zoller appears in several candidates, so the committee should avoid duplicate recognition
Credit for the original lattice proposal versus the experiments is somewhat entangled

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics established strong coupling of superconducting qubits to microwave resonators, providing the architecture for dispersive readout, gates and error-corrected processors. It has had very broad technological and scientific impact, and its foundations are closely tied to quantum optics ideas I know well.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf are the proposal-plus-experiment core. Yale colleagues such as Devoret, Girvin and Huang are major contributors, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits touches the same field, so the allocation is not fully clean.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across many laboratories and companies. Recognition is timely, but the recent circuit-based prize may make the committee cautious about returning so soon.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits (as I recall it, not verified here)
Whether other Yale contributors should share the credit

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays use optical tweezers and Rydberg blockade to build controllable many-body quantum systems and high-fidelity gates, enabling quantum simulation and early neutral-atom processors. The work is original and technically demanding, and it builds directly on atomic physics methods.
assessment.attribution: Lukin, Browaeys and Saffman each made central contributions to blockade-based gates and large arrays, while Zoller's early proposals and the Greiner and Bakr tweezer work add complexity. Choosing three names omits substantive contributors.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly advancing and well reproduced, but still evolving, with error correction and scale demonstrations ongoing. This is somewhat early compared with the top-ranked candidates.
uncertainties: Maturity: the field is still changing quickly
Attribution is spread over many groups

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Single colour-centre spins, especially NV centres in diamond, were shown to support optical readout and coherent control at room temperature, leading to solid-state qubits, nanoscale sensing and quantum network nodes. This resonates with my own work on coherent control in doped crystals, and its sensing impact is broad.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated optical detection of single NV spins; Awschalom contributed coherent control and the wider colour-centre programme; Lukin led sensing and network developments. Walsworth and others also contributed, so the choice is a judgement among several strong contributors.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently and used widely, though some applications such as sensing and networks are still developing.
uncertainties: The collective credit is spread over multiple groups
Potential for compound recognition of qubit and sensing aspects

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The study of strongly interacting Fermi gases, including the BEC-BCS crossover, unitary gases and superfluidity in a controllable setting, has been an important advance connecting atomic physics with condensed matter and nuclear physics.
assessment.attribution: Grimm, Salomon and Ketterle led key demonstrations of molecular condensates, fermionic superfluidity and vortices. Ketterle is already a laureate (2001), which complicates the configuration, and Jin's early death removes a central contributor, a point I recall rather than verify.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and mature, although the importance has more of a gradual character than a single discovery, and the time since the key experiments is now long.
uncertainties: The absence of Deborah Jin from any eligible credit

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Solid-state femtosecond lasers, from Ti:sapphire gain media to Kerr-lens modelocking and semiconductor saturable absorbers, made ultrafast sources compact and practical, enabling frequency combs, spectroscopy and attosecond science. As a laser spectroscopist I value the lasting enabling impact.
assessment.attribution: Moulton introduced Ti:sapphire, Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens modelocking, and Keller developed SESAM modelocking; these are distinct contributions and the allocation is plausible with three names. Other credible contributors exist, for example Spence, Kuizenga and others, which I do not verify.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed, but the major ultrafast prizes in 1999, 2018 and 2023 mean the committee may regard this as already recognised in effect.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier ultrafast and laser prizes
Whether the invention is better treated as technology than as a discovery
